entries.title: Students in a course
entries.citation: George Klir, Facets of Systems Science, 2nd ed. (2001), Ch. 2, Table 2.1 and Table 2.2, Fig. 2.2a
entries.teaches: An equivalence relation on a named set, given by Klir as a set, as a matrix, and as a node-edge diagram — the same system in three registers, with the relation partitioning the set into equivalence classes.

entries.title: Goal-oriented systems — the Informationless paradigm
entries.citation: George Klir, Facets of Systems Science, 2nd ed. (2001), Ch. 10 §10.2, Fig. 10.1
entries.teaches: The most restrictive of Klir's four goal-oriented paradigms: the goal-seeking element emits its variable blind, receiving neither the input nor the output it is trying to influence.

entries.title: Goal-oriented systems — the Feedback paradigm
entries.citation: George Klir, Facets of Systems Science, 2nd ed. (2001), Ch. 10 §10.2, Fig. 10.1
entries.teaches: The goal-seeking element reads the output variable, so it can react to undesirable changes in the output but has no mechanism for anticipating them.

entries.title: Goal-oriented systems — the Feedforward paradigm
entries.citation: George Klir, Facets of Systems Science, 2nd ed. (2001), Ch. 10 §10.2, Fig. 10.1
entries.teaches: The goal-seeking element reads the input variable, letting it anticipate the output rather than only react to it.

entries.title: Goal-oriented systems — the Full-information paradigm
entries.citation: George Klir, Facets of Systems Science, 2nd ed. (2001), Ch. 10 §10.2, Fig. 10.1
entries.teaches: The least restrictive paradigm: the goal-seeking element reads both the input and the output, combining anticipation with reaction.

entries.title: The two-thing system — a acts on b
entries.citation: Mario Bunge, Treatise on Basic Philosophy, Vol. 4: A World of Systems (1979), Ch. 1 §1.2, Definition 1.2, Example, Fig. 1.2
entries.teaches: The simplest possible system in Bunge's words: two connected things in an environment lumped into a single thing, with the internal structure a▷b — a acts on b, and not conversely.

entries.title: The two-thing system — b acts on a
entries.citation: Mario Bunge, Treatise on Basic Philosophy, Vol. 4: A World of Systems (1979), Ch. 1 §1.2, Definition 1.2, Example, Fig. 1.2
entries.teaches: The same composition and environment as its siblings, with the internal structure reversed to b▷a — showing that structure, not composition, is what distinguishes these systems.

entries.title: The two-thing system — a and b act on each other
entries.citation: Mario Bunge, Treatise on Basic Philosophy, Vol. 4: A World of Systems (1979), Ch. 1 §1.2, Definition 1.2, Example, Fig. 1.2
entries.teaches: The same composition and environment again, with the reciprocal internal structure a⋈b — the third and last of the conceivable internal structures on two things.
